probes.query: Find the public `escape` function in the globset crate that turns a literal string into a glob pattern by bracketing meta characters.
expectedFacts: globset::escape wraps each of the glob meta characters ? * [ ] { } in square brackets (e.g. * becomes [*]) while passing all other characters through unchanged
probes.author: rust-author
probes.notes: grep -n 'pub fn escape(s: &str)' crates/globset/src/lib.rs -> crates/globset/src/lib.rs:1035. Body (lib.rs:1035-1052) brackets ? * [ ] { } and passes other chars through. Note there is ALSO a crates/cli/src/escape.rs:26 `pub fn escape(bytes: &[u8])` (shell escaping) — distinct symbol; the query anchors on 'globset' + 'glob pattern' to disambiguate.

probes.query: Where is the Sink trait defined and what is the signature of the method the searcher calls every time it finds a match?
expectedFacts: The Sink trait declares `fn matched(&mut self, _searcher: &Searcher, _mat: &SinkMatch<'_>) -> Result<bool, Self::Error>`; returning Ok(false) stops the search and Ok(true) continues it
probes.author: rust-author
probes.notes: grep -n 'pub trait Sink {' crates/searcher/src/sink.rs -> sink.rs:102. grep -n 'fn matched(' crates/searcher/src/sink.rs -> sink.rs:124. Signature + return-value semantics confirmed in the doc comment at sink.rs:110-124.

probes.query: When ripgrep hits a non-fatal error and wants the process to exit non-zero, which macro does it call to print 'rg: <msg>' to stderr and flip the errored flag?
expectedFacts: The err_message! macro calls crate::messages::set_errored() and then delegates to message!, which (if messages are enabled) expands to eprintln_locked! — so err_message! is a three-macro chain (err_message -> message -> eprintln_locked) that prints the 'rg: ' prefix to stderr
probes.author: rust-author
probes.notes: grep -n 'macro_rules! err_message' crates/core/messages.rs -> messages.rs:82. err_message! (msgs.rs:82-87) calls set_errored() then message!; message! (msgs.rs:71-78) calls eprintln_locked!; eprintln_locked! (msgs.rs:33) writes 'rg: ' prefix. HARD: the answer is a #[macro_export] macro_rules! definition, not a fn — symbol search keyed on 'errored flag'+'non-fatal error' must resolve the macro, and the behaviour spans a 3-macro expansion chain that lexical/AST tools struggle to follow.

probes.query: Trace how the `-S`/`--smart-case` command-line flag ends up turning on smart-case matching in the regex builder.
expectedFacts: The SmartCase flag's update() method sets args.case = CaseMode::Smart in defs.rs, and hiargs.rs later maps CaseMode::Smart to builder.case_smart(true) when configuring the matcher
probes.author: rust-author
probes.notes: grep -n 'struct SmartCase;' crates/core/flags/defs.rs -> defs.rs:6141; 'impl Flag for SmartCase' -> defs.rs:6143; update() sets `args.case = CaseMode::Smart` (defs.rs:6178-6182). grep -n 'CaseMode::Smart => builder.case_smart' crates/core/flags/hiargs.rs -> hiargs.rs:419 and hiargs.rs:471. HARD: SmartCase is one of 104 unit-struct `impl Flag for X` blocks; the connection from the CLI string '--smart-case' to behaviour goes through a trait method override (Flag::update) then a separate CaseMode match in another file — dynamic-dispatch + cross-file flow.

probes.query: Each ripgrep CLI flag is its own type implementing a shared trait. Where is that trait declared, and where is the master list of every flag instance that the parser iterates over?
expectedFacts: The Flag trait is declared in flags/mod.rs and the FLAGS constant in flags/defs.rs is a `&[&dyn Flag]` slice holding one trait object per flag (e.g. &SmartCase, &MaxColumns), which the parser and doc generators iterate with FLAGS.iter()
probes.author: rust-author
probes.notes: grep -n 'trait Flag:' crates/core/flags/mod.rs -> mod.rs:71 (`trait Flag: Debug + Send + Sync + ...`). grep -n 'pub(super) const FLAGS:' crates/core/flags/defs.rs -> defs.rs:44 (`pub(super) const FLAGS: &[&dyn Flag] = &[`). FLAGS.iter() usages confirmed (defs.rs:7632 etc). Two-file flow: trait declaration in mod.rs, dyn-trait-object registry table in defs.rs.

probes.query: How does ripgrep transparently read a compressed file like foo.gz? Find the reader type that shells out to an external decompression program, and the fallback it uses when no matching decompressor is configured.
expectedFacts: DecompressionReader::new builds via DecompressionReaderBuilder; when no decompression command matches the path it falls back to new_passthru, which opens the file directly (rdr: Err(file)) and reads it without spawning a child process
probes.author: rust-author
probes.notes: grep -n 'pub struct DecompressionReader {' crates/cli/src/decompress.rs -> decompress.rs:332. `new` at decompress.rs:352 delegates to DecompressionReaderBuilder::new().build(path). `new_passthru` at decompress.rs:361 returns DecompressionReader { rdr: Err(file) } (passthru, no child process). Confirmed via sed -n '352,395p'.

probes.query: ripgrep can memory-map files for searching but deliberately avoids mmap on one specific operating system. Which OS, where is that decision made, and what does it do instead?
expectedFacts: In MmapChoice::open, when cfg!(target_os = "macos") is true the method returns None (skipping the memory map) so the searcher falls back to buffered reads, because memory maps on macOS are noted as not being great
probes.author: rust-author
probes.notes: grep -n 'pub(crate) fn open(' crates/searcher/src/searcher/mmap.rs -> mmap.rs:65. grep -n 'target_os = "macos"' -> mmap.rs:73, which `return None;` with comment 'memory maps on macOS aren't great'. is_enabled()/Auto vs Never at mmap.rs ~98-110. Behavioral: the answer is a guard branch (cfg! check returning None) inside open(), not a named symbol.

probes.query: ripgrep has two binary-data strategies: one stops the search, the other replaces the offending byte. Find both constructors and explain the difference in what happens to the matched byte.
expectedFacts: BinaryDetection::quit(byte) makes the search stop when the byte is seen, while BinaryDetection::convert(byte) replaces that byte with the configured line terminator; convert has no effect when the file is searched via a memory map
probes.author: rust-author
probes.notes: grep -n 'pub fn convert(binary_byte' crates/searcher/src/searcher/mod.rs -> mod.rs:95; quit at mod.rs:79. quit -> line_buffer::BinaryDetection::Quit; convert -> Convert (replaces byte with line terminator; 'no effect' under mmap per doc at mod.rs:91-94). quit_byte/convert_byte accessors at mod.rs:102/112.

probes.query: Find the LRU cache that ripgrep uses to cache compiled regex objects across files so it doesn't recompile the same pattern.
probes.author: rust-author
probes.notes: Verified ABSENT: grep -rin --include='*.rs' -e 'LruCache' -e 'lru_cache' -e 'fn evict' -e 'cache eviction' crates/ -> 0 results. ripgrep compiles the pattern once up front and reuses the Matcher; there is no LRU regex cache. Plausible-sounding feature that does not exist.

probes.author: rust-author
